'''Cambridge''' is a [[List of United Kingdom Parliament constituencies|constituency]]{{#tag:ref|A [[borough constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer)|group= n}} represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|UK Parliament]] since [[2015 United Kingdom general election|2015]] by [[Daniel Zeichner]] of the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]].{{#tag:ref|As with all constituencies, the constituency elects one [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) by the [[first past the post]] system of election at least every five years.|group= n}} Centred on the [[College town|university city]] of [[Cambridge]], it is one of the country's oldest continuously constituted constituencies. It was created in 1295 and returned two [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Members of Parliament]] (MPs) and was represented in the [[House of Commons of England]] until 1707, then in the [[House of Commons of Great Britain]] from 1707 to 1800, and then in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the United Kingdom from 1801 to 1885. From 1885 onwards, the seat has elected one MP. It was held by the Conservatives from 1967 to 1992, since when it has been represented alternately by both Labour and the Liberal Democrats. In the [[2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum|2016 referendum]] to leave the European Union, the [[results of the 2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum by constituency|constituency voted]] 73.8% to remain.{{cite web |url=https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1wTK5dV2_YjCMsUYlwg0l48uWWf44sKgG8uFVMv5OWlA/edit#gid=893960794 |title=Revised estimates of leave vote in Westminster constituencies |access-date=26 October 2016 |archive-date=15 March 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170315003907/https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1wTK5dV2_YjCMsUYlwg0l48uWWf44sKgG8uFVMv5OWlA/edit#gid=893960794 |url-status=live }} ==Constituency profile== The current constituency covers the majority of the city of [[Cambridge]], including the areas of Arbury (which contains some social housing), [[Chesterton, Cambridge|Chesterton]], [[Newnham, Cambridgeshire|Newnham]], [[Cherry Hinton]] and the village of [[Trumpington]]; but the city's Queen Edith's ward (which includes [[Addenbrooke's Hospital]] and [[Homerton College]]) is in the neighbouring [[South Cambridgeshire (UK Parliament constituency)|South Cambridgeshire]] constituency. Residents are healthier and wealthier than the UK average.Electoral Calculus https://www.electoralcalculus.co.uk/fcgi-bin/seatdetails.py?seat=Cambridge == History == === Overview of results before 1992 === Cambridge returned two Members to Parliament from 1295 until 1885, using the [[Preferential block voting|bloc vote]] system.{{cite book|chapter=The city of Cambridge: Parliamentary representation|title=A History of the County of Cambridge and the Isle of Ely: Volume 3, the City and University of Cambridge|editor=J P C Roach|year=1959|chapter-url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/cambs/vol3/pp68-76|access-date=6 December 2019|archive-date=6 December 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191206124506/https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/cambs/vol3/pp68-76|url-status=live}} These were generally townsmen who were involved in local government, with at least sixty mayors of Cambridge having served as MP by 1621. Under the [[Redistribution of Seats Act 1885]] representation was reduced to one member, using the [[first-past-the-post]] system, with effect from the [[1885 United Kingdom general election|1885 general election]]. From 1910 to 1992, Cambridge was won by the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservatives]], save for 1945 to 1950 and 1966 to 1968, when it was [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]]-held with small majorities. ;Related extra representation 1603–1950 Historically, the city of Cambridge retained some electors, and was often the source of MPs to a second constituency, for [[Cambridge University (UK Parliament constituency)|Cambridge University]], covering all successful alumni in its electorate. The university seat was created in 1603 as part of the scheme of [[University constituency|University constituencies]]. Its MPs included [[Isaac Newton]], [[William Pitt the Younger]], [[Henry Temple, 3rd Viscount Palmerston|Lord Palmerston]], [[Sir George Stokes, 1st Baronet|George Stokes]], [[Richard Claverhouse Jebb|Richard Jebb]], and [[Archibald Hill]] before abolition in 1950. === Overview of results since 1992 === In 1992, Cambridge was won by [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]]'s [[Anne Campbell (politician)|Anne Campbell]], who held onto the seat for 13 years (three Parliamentary terms). In 2005, it was taken by [[David Howarth]] of the [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrats]], the first time the party (including its two forerunner parties) had taken the seat since the [[1906 United Kingdom general election|1906]] Liberal-progressive [[Landslide victory|landslide]]; his successor, [[Julian Huppert]], held the seat with an increased majority in the 2010 general election. In 2015, Huppert was unseated by the Labour candidate, [[Daniel Zeichner]], who took the seat with a thin majority of 599 votes. The 2015 result gave the seat the 7th-smallest majority of Labour's 232 seats by percentage of majority.{{cite web |url=http://www.ukpolitical.info/labour-mps-elected-2015.htm |title=Labour Members of Parliament 2015 |website=UK Political.info |archive-date=2018-09-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180929214847/http://www.ukpolitical.info/labour-mps-elected-2015.htm |url-status=live}} Zeichner went on to hold the seat at the 2017 and 2019 elections with comfortable majorities. ;Most recent results of other parties In 2015, three other parties candidates kept their [[deposit (politics)|deposits]], by winning more than 5% of the vote. In order of public preference, these candidates stood for the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservatives]], [[Green Party of England and Wales|Green Party]] and [[UKIP]], respectively. ;Turnout since 1918 Turnout at general elections has ranged between 86.48% in 1950 to 60.6% in 2001. == Boundaries and boundary changes == === 1868–1918 === * The Borough of Cambridge, plus the village of Chesterton.{{Cite web|url=http://www.visionofbritain.org.uk/maps/sheet/bc_reports_1868/Cambridge_1868|title=H.M.S.O. Milton & Waterbeach.{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule I Part 2 Eastern region}} The bulk of the electorate, including the city of [[Ely, Cambridgeshire|Ely]] and the town of [[Soham]], was derived from about two-thirds of the abolished constituency of [[South East Cambridgeshire (UK Parliament constituency)|South East Cambridgeshire]], with the addition of areas from [[North East Cambridgeshire (UK Parliament constituency)|North East Cambridgeshire]] ([[Littleport]], [[Sutton-in-the-Isle]] and Downham Villages) and [[South Cambridgeshire (UK Parliament constituency)|South Cambridgeshire]] ([[Cottenham]]). {{Short description|Parliamentary constituency in the United Kingdom since 1974}} {{Use dmy dates|date=March 2020}} {{Infobox UK constituency main |name = Braintree |parliament = uk |image = {{maplink|frame=yes|frame-align=center|plain=yes|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Braintree (UK Parliament constituency)}}|frame-height=200|frame-width=250}} |caption = Boundaries since 2024 |image2 = [[File:East of England - Braintree constituency.svg|215px|alt=Map of constituency]] |caption2 = Boundary of Braintree in the East of England |year = 1974 |abolished = |type = County |previous = [[Maldon (UK Parliament constituency)|Maldon]] |next = |population = 97,840 (2011 census)<ref>{{cite web |title=Braintree: Usual Resident Population, 2011 |url=http://neighbourhood.statistics.gov.uk/dissemination/LeadTableView.do?a=7&b=6507764&c=&d=27&e=62&g=6430187&i=1001x1003x1032x1004&o=362&m=0&r=1&s=1422104706393&enc=1&dsFamilyId=2473 |work=Neighbourhood Statistics |publisher=Office for National Statistics |access-date=2 February 2015}}</ref> |electorate = 75,662 (2023)<ref>{{cite web |url= https://boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk/2023-review/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition-eastern/#lg_braintree-cc-75662 |title= The 2023 Review of Parliamentary Constituency Boundaries in England – Volume two: Constituency names, designations and composition – Eastern |publisher=Boundary Commission for England |access-date=26 June 2024 |df=dmy }}</ref> |towns = [[Braintree, Essex|Braintree]], [[Halstead, Essex|Halstead]] |mp = [[James Cleverly]] |party = [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] |region = England |county = [[Essex]] |european = East of England |elects_howmany = One }} '''Braintree''' is a [[Constituencies of the Parliament of the United Kingdom|constituency]]{{#tag:ref|A [[county constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer)|group= n}} in [[Essex]] represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|UK Parliament]] since [[2015 United Kingdom general election|2015]] by [[James Cleverly]], a member of the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]].
Cleverly is a former [[Chairman of the Conservative Party]] and currently the [[Home Secretary|Secretary of State for the Home Department]]. He was also the former [[Foreign Secretary|Secretary of State for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office]] and [[Secretary of State for Education]].
The constituency was created for the [[February 1974 United Kingdom general election|February 1974 general election]].{{#tag:ref|As with all constituencies, the constituency elects one [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) by the [[first past the post]] system of election at least every five years.|group= n}}
==Constituency profile== The constituency includes the town of [[Braintree, Essex|Braintree]] at its southern end, and a large area of rural Essex to the north. == History == The seat was created for the [[February 1974 United Kingdom general election|February 1974 general election]], largely from the majority of the constituency of [[Maldon (UK Parliament constituency)|Maldon]], including the towns of [[Braintree, Essex|Braintree]] and [[Witham]]. It underwent a major redistribution for the [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010 general election]] when [[Witham (UK Parliament constituency)|Witham]] was formed as a separate constituency. This resulted in making the seat safer for the Conservatives.
The former Leader of the House [[Tony Newton, Baron Newton of Braintree|Tony Newton]] held the seat for the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservatives]] from its creation in 1974 until 1997 when [[Alan Hurst (politician)|Alan Hurst]] defeated Newton to gain the seat for [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]]. [[Brooks Newmark]] defeated Hurst in 2005 to regain the seat for the Conservatives, and held it until he stood down in 2015, being succeeded by [[James Cleverly]], also a Conservative.<ref>Will Lodge, [https://www.eadt.co.uk/news/election-2015-conservatives-extend-lead-in-braintree-as-james-cleverly-takes-over-as-mp-1-4065626 "Election 2015: Conservatives extend lead in Braintree as James Cleverly takes over as MP"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190725172306/https://www.eadt.co.uk/news/election-2015-conservatives-extend-lead-in-braintree-as-james-cleverly-takes-over-as-mp-1-4065626 |date=25 July 2019 }}, East Anglian Daily Times, 8 May 2015</ref>
==Boundaries and boundary changes==
=== 1974–1983 ===
* The Urban Districts of Braintree and Bocking, and Witham; * The Rural District of Braintree; and * The Rural District of Chelmsford civil parishes of Boreham, Broomfield, Chignall, Good Easter, Great and Little Leighs, Great Waltham, Little Waltham, Mashbury, Pleshey, Roxwell, Springfield, and Writtle.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1970/1674/contents/made/data.htm|title=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 1970|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|access-date=2019-09-09}}</ref>
''Formed largely from the existing constituency of [[Maldon (UK Parliament constituency)|Maldon]]. The northern part of the [[Chelmsford Rural District|Rural District of Chelmsford]] was transferred from [[Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|Chelmsford]] and a small part of the [[Braintree Rural District|Rural District of Braintree]] was previously in [[Saffron Walden (UK Parliament constituency)|Saffron Walden]].''
=== 1983–1997 ===
* The District of Braintree wards of Black Notley, Bocking North, Bocking South, Braintree Central, Braintree East, Braintree West, Coggeshall, Cressing, Hatfield Peverel, Kelvedon, Panfield, Rayne, Terling, Three Fields, Witham Central, Witham Chipping Hill, Witham North, Witham Silver End and Rivenhall, Witham South, and Witham West; and * The Borough of Chelmsford wards of Broomfield and Chignall, Good Easter Mashbury and Roxwell, Great and Little Leighs and Little Waltham, Great Waltham and Pleshey, and Writtle.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1983/417/contents/made/data.htm|title=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 1983|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|access-date=2019-09-09}}</ref>
''Following changes to the structure of local authorities in 1974, the seat was largely unchanged, with just the Boreham and Springfield ward of Chelmsford Borough being transferred to the Chelmsford constituency.''
=== 1997–2010 ===
* The District of Braintree wards of Black Notley, Bocking North, Bocking South, Braintree Central, Braintree East, Braintree West, Coggeshall, Cressing, Earls Colne, Gosfield, Hatfield Peveril, Kelvedon, Panfield, Rayne, Terling, Three Fields, Witham Central, Witham Chipping Hill, Witham North, Witham Silver End and Rivenhall, Witham South, and Witham West.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1995/1626/made/data.htm|title=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 1995|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|language=en|access-date=2019-09-09}}</ref>
''The parts in the Borough of Chelmsford now included in the new constituency of [[West Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|West Chelmsford]]. Two small wards (Earls Colne and Gosfield) transferred from [[Saffron Walden (UK Parliament constituency)|Saffron Walden]].''
=== 2010–2024 === * The District of Braintree wards of Bocking Blackwater, Bocking North, Bocking South, Braintree Central, Braintree East, Braintree South, Bumpstead, Cressing and Stisted, Gosfield and Greenstead Green, Great Notley and Braintree West, Halstead St Andrews, Halstead Trinity, Hedingham and Maplestead, Panfield, Rayne, Stour Valley North, Stour Valley South, The Three Colnes, Three Fields, Upper Colne, and Yeldham.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2007/1681/made/data.htm|title=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 2007|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|access-date=2019-09-09}}</ref>
''The 2010 redistribution saw a major change, with southern and western areas, including the town of [[Witham]], forming the basis of the new County Constituency of [[Witham (UK Parliament constituency)|Witham]]. Extended northwards, gaining the District of Braintree wards previously in Saffron Walden, including the town of [[Halstead]].''
=== 2024–present === Following the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency is as follows (as they existed on 1 December 2020):
* The District of Braintree wards of: Bocking Blackwater; Bocking North; Bocking South; Braintree Central & Beckers Green; Braintree South; Braintree West; Bumpstead; Gosfield & Greenstead Green; Great Notley & Black Notley; Halstead St. Andrew’s; Halstead Trinity; Hedingham; Rayne; Stour Valley North; Stour Valley South; Three Fields; Yeldham.
* The District of Uttlesford wards of: Felsted & Stebbing; The Sampfords.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule I Part 2 Eastern region}}</ref>
''Minor changes – the two Uttlesford District wards were transferred from [[Saffron Walden (UK Parliament constituency)|Saffron Walden]] (renamed [[North West Essex (UK Parliament constituency)|North West Essex]]), offset by a net loss to [[Witham (UK Parliament constituency)|Witham]] mainly due to revision of ward boundaries.''
==Members of Parliament== {| class="wikitable" |- !colspan="2"|Election!!Member<ref>{{cite web|title=Braintree 1974–|url=https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/constituencies/braintree|website=[[Hansard|Parliamentary Debates (Hansard)]]|access-date=2 February 2015}}</ref><ref name="rayment">{{Rayment-hc|b|5|date=March 2012}}</ref> !Party |- |style="background-color: {{party color|Conservative Party (UK)}}" | | [[February 1974 United Kingdom general election|Feb 1974]] | [[Tony Newton, Baron Newton of Braintree|Tony Newton]] | [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] |- |style="background-color: {{party color|Labour Party (UK)}}" | | [[1997 United Kingdom general election|1997]] | [[Alan Hurst (politician)|Alan Hurst]] | [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] |- |style="background-color: {{party color|Conservative Party (UK)}}" | | [[2005 United Kingdom general election|2005]] | [[Brooks Newmark]] | [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] |- |style="background-color: {{party color|Conservative Party (UK)}}" | | [[2015 United Kingdom general election|2015]] | [[James Cleverly]] | [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] |}

{{EngvarB|date=October 2013}} {{Use dmy dates|date=October 2013}} {{Infobox UK constituency main |name = Thurrock |parliament = uk |image = {{maplink|frame=yes|frame-align=center|plain=yes|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Thurrock (UK Parliament constituency)}}|frame-height=200|frame-width=250}} |caption = Boundaries since 2024 |image2 = [[File:East of England - Thurrock constituency.svg|215px|alt=Map of constituency]] |caption2 = Boundary of Thurrock in the East of England |year = 1945 |abolished = |type = Borough |elects_howmany = One |previous = [[South East Essex (UK Parliament constituency)|South East Essex]] |next = |electorate = 73,347 (2023)<ref>{{cite web |url= https://boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk/2023-review/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition-eastern/#lg_thurrock-bc-73347 |title= The 2023 Review of Parliamentary Constituency Boundaries in England – Volume two: Constituency names, designations and composition – Eastern |publisher=Boundary Commission for England |access-date=27 June 2024 |df=dmy }}</ref> |mp = [[Jen Craft]] |party = [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] |region = England |county = [[Essex]] |towns = [[Grays, Essex|Grays]], [[Tilbury]], [[South Ockendon]] and [[Chafford Hundred|Chafford]] }} '''Thurrock''' is a [[List of United Kingdom Parliament constituencies|constituency]]{{#tag:ref|A [[county constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer)|group= n}} represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|UK Parliament]] since 2024 by [[Jen Craft]] of the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]].{{#tag:ref|As with all constituencies, the constituency elects one Member of Parliament (MP) by the [[first past the post]] system of election at least every five years.|group= n}}
== Constituency profile == This industrial Essex seat, east of London, includes the towns of [[Grays, Essex|Grays]], [[Tilbury]] and [[Purfleet]], and 18 miles of the north bank of the Thames.
Historically known for quarrying and heavy industry, it is now a retail destination thanks to the [[Lakeside Shopping Centre]]. Retail and distribution are big employers, while Tilbury Power Station has closed and Coryton oil refinery is being redeveloped as a business park. Tilbury is also London's major port, handling millions of tonnes of cargo a year and is a major cruise ship terminal.
Workless claimants, registered jobseekers, were in November 2012 higher than the national average of 3.8%, at 4.8% of the population based on a statistical compilation by ''[[The Guardian]]''. The regional average for the Eastern England region was considerably lower, at 3.2% of the population.<ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/news/datablog/2010/nov/17/unemployment-and-employment-statistics-economics Unemployment claimants by constituency] ''[[The Guardian]]''</ref>
== History == '''History of boundaries'''
The seat was created from [[South East Essex (UK Parliament constituency)|South East Essex]] as a result of the interim redistribution carried out for the [[1945 United Kingdom general election|1945 general election]]. It remained unchanged until the redistribution following the reorganisation of local authorities under the [[Local Government Act 1972]] (not coming into force until the [[1983 United Kingdom general election|1983 general election]]), when it lost northern parts to the new constituency of [[Billericay (UK Parliament constituency)|Billericay]]. There was a small change for the 2010 general election, when East Tilbury was included in the new constituency of [[South Basildon and East Thurrock (UK Parliament constituency)|South Basildon and East Thurrock]].
;History of results
All campaigns since the seat's 1945 inception have resulted in a minimum of 26.8% of votes at each election for the main two parties, with [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] or the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservatives]] alternating between first and second place. The third-placed party's share of the vote has fluctuated between 31.7% and 20.1% of the vote for [[UKIP]] and between 8.1% and 21.7% in the case of the [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrats]] and that party's predecessors. The seat attracted two candidates in 1959 and seven in 2015.
Thurrock was for 38 years from and including 1945 a [[safe seat|large-majority]] Labour seat in parliamentary elections. The post-[[Falklands War]] election in 1983 gave a majority of less than 4% of the vote to a recently-split Labour Party (the breakaway faction, the [[Social Democratic Party (United Kingdom)|SDP]], came third). A Conservative gained Thurrock in 1987 with a small majority. In 1992, it was regained by a Labour candidate, [[Andrew MacKinlay]]. During his tenure as MP, MacKinlay was criticised for his questioning technique used on weapons expert [[David Kelly (weapons expert)|Dr. David Kelly]].
In the [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010 general election]], a Conservative gained the seat, with [[Jackie Doyle-Price]] being elected as the MP on a majority of 92 votes, the third most marginal in that election.<ref>The 2010 marginality of the result placed the seat immediately behind the majorities of [[Dan Byles]] (Con), 54 votes and Michelle Gildernew (SF), 2 votes</ref> The 2015 result gave the seat the 8th most marginal majority of the Conservative Party's 331 seats by percentage of majority.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ukpolitical.info/conservative-mps-elected-2015.htm |title=Conservative Members of Parliament 2015 |website=UK Political.info |access-date=2017-02-12 |archive-date=2017-06-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170608170823/http://www.ukpolitical.info/conservative-mps-elected-2015.htm |url-status=live}}</ref> In that 2015 election fewer than 1,000 votes separated the top three parties: Conservative, Labour and UKIP. The seat has had [[bellwether]] outcome status since 1997.
In [[2017 United Kingdom general election|2017]], the seat was number 1 on UKIP's 2017 target list, the party only needing a 0.98% swing to win the seat from third place if the previous result were repeated. The constituency was also at number 7 on Labour's target list, with a 0.54% swing needed for their candidate to win the seat. In the event, the swing to Labour was around 0.2% and Doyle-Price held the seat by a mere 345 votes, making it the 26th-closest nationally (of 650 seats).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/insights/ge2017-marginal-seats-and-turnout/|title=GE2017: Marginal seats and turnout|last=Library|first=House of Commons|date=23 June 2017|publisher=Commons Library}}</ref> This was also the third consecutive occasion that Thurrock had been held or won very narrowly. At the [[2019 United Kingdom general election|2019 general election]], Doyle-Price's vote share increased by 19.1%, the largest increase in vote share achieved by any Conservative candidate in the United Kingdom at that election, and her majority rose to 11,482 votes, making it a safe Conservative seat.<ref name="TimesGuide19">{{cite book |title=The Times Guide to the House of Commons 2019 |date=2020 |publisher=Times Books |location=Glasgow |isbn=978-0-00-839258-1 |pages=53 & 360}}</ref>
;Prominent frontbenchers Dr [[Oonagh McDonald]] was Opposition Spokesman on Defence from 1981 to 1983, and then Opposition Spokesman on Treasury and Economic Affairs from 1983 to 1987.
== Boundaries and boundary changes == [[File:Thurrock1945.png|thumb|300x300px|Thurrock in Essex, showing boundaries used from 1945 to 1983.]] {{maplink|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Thurrock (UK Parliament constituency) 2010}}|frame=yes|frame-height=250|text=Map of boundaries 2010-2024}}
=== 1945–1983 ===
* The Urban District of Thurrock.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Boundaries of parliamentary constituencies 1885-1972;|last=Craig, Fred W. S.|date=1972|publisher=Political Reference Publications|isbn=0900178094|location=Chichester|oclc=539011}}</ref>
''The [[House of Commons (Redistribution of Seats) Act 1944]] set up Boundaries Commissions to carry out periodic reviews of the distribution of parliamentary constituencies. It also authorised an initial review to subdivide abnormally large constituencies in time for the [[1945 United Kingdom general election|1945 election]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gay|first=Oonagh|date=2010-07-28|title=The Rules for the Redistribution of Seats- history and reform|url=https://researchbriefings.parliament.uk/ResearchBriefing/Summary/SN05628}}</ref> This was implemented by the Redistribution of Seats Order 1945 under which [[South East Essex (UK Parliament constituency)|South East Essex]] was divided into two constituencies. As a consequence, the new '''Thurrock''' Division of Essex was formed, comprising the [[Thurrock Urban District|Urban District of Thurrock]] (created largely from amalgamating the Urban Districts of Grays Thurrock and Tilbury and the Rural District of Orsett).''
=== 1983–2010 ===
* The Borough of Thurrock wards of Aveley, Belhus, Chadwell St Mary, East Tilbury, Grays Thurrock North, Grays Thurrock Town, Little Thurrock, Ockendon, Stifford, Tilbury, and West Thurrock.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1983/417/contents/made/data.htm|title=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 1983|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|access-date=2019-09-07}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1995/1626/made/data.htm|title=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 1995|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|language=en|access-date=2019-09-07}}</ref>
''Northern areas transferred to the re-established constituency of [[Billericay (UK Parliament constituency)|Billericay]].''
=== 2010–2024 ===
* The Borough of Thurrock wards of Aveley and Uplands, Belhus, Chadwell St Mary, Chafford and North Stifford, Grays Riverside, Grays Thurrock, Little Thurrock Blackshots, Little Thurrock Rectory, Ockendon, South Chafford, Stifford Clays, Tilbury Riverside and Thurrock Park, Tilbury St Chads, West Thurrock, and South Stifford.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2007/1681/made/data.htm|title=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 2007|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|access-date=2019-09-07}}</ref>
''Following a redistribution of local authority wards, [[East Tilbury]] was transferred to the new constituency of [[South Basildon and East Thurrock (UK Parliament constituency)|South Basildon and East Thurrock]].''
=== Current === Further to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency was reduced to meet the electorate size requirements, with the transfer to [[South Basildon and East Thurrock (UK Parliament constituency)|South Basildon and East Thurrock]] of the [[Chadwell St Mary]] ward.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule I Part 2 Eastern region}}</ref>

Maldon constituency.svg|215px|alt=Map of constituency]] |caption2 = Boundary of Maldon in the East of England |year = 2010 |mp = [[To be confirmed|TBC]] |party = [[To be confirmed|TBC]] |towns = [[Maldon]], [[Burnham-on-Crouch]], [[South Woodham Ferrers]] |abolished = |type = County |previous = [[Maldon and East Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|Maldon and East Chelmsford]], [[Rayleigh (UK Parliament constituency)|Rayleigh]] and [[West Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|West Chelmsford]] |next = |electorate = 76,794 (2023){{cite web |url= https://boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk/2023-review/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition-eastern/#lg_maldon-cc-76794 |title= The 2023 Review of Parliamentary Constituency Boundaries in England – Volume two: Constituency names, designations and composition – Eastern |publisher=Boundary Commission for England |access-date=26 June 2024 |df=dmy }} |region = England |county = [[Essex]] |european = East of England |elects_howmany = One |year2 = 1885 |abolished2 = 1983 |type2 = County |previous2 = [[East Essex (UK Parliament constituency)|East Essex]], Maldon (Parliamentary Borough) |next2 = [[Colchester South and Maldon (UK Parliament constituency)|Colchester South and Maldon]] and [[Rochford (UK Parliament constituency)|Rochford]] |elects_howmany2 = One |year3 = 1332 |abolished3 = 1885 |type3 = Borough |previous3 = |elects_howmany3 = 1332–1868: Two
1868–1885: One |next3 = Maldon (county constituency) }} '''Maldon''' is a [[Constituencies of the Parliament of the United Kingdom|constituency]]{{#tag:ref|A [[county constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer).|group= n}} in [[Essex]] represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|UK Parliament]] since its recreation in [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010]] by [[John Whittingdale|Sir John Whittingdale]], a [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]].{{#tag:ref|As with all constituencies, the constituency elects one [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) by the [[first past the post]] system of election at least every five years.|group= n}} ==Constituency profile== Maldon covers a rural area of Essex including the [[Dengie Peninsula]]. The main settlements are [[Maldon]] and [[Burnham-on-Crouch]] on the coast, and the new town of [[South Woodham Ferrers]]. The seat is slightly wealthier than the UK average.Electoral Calculus https://www.electoralcalculus.co.uk/fcgi-bin/seatdetails.py?seat=Maldon ==History== The Parliamentary Borough of Maldon, which included the parish of [[Heybridge, Maldon|Heybridge]], had sent two members to the [[Parliament of England]] since it was founded in 1332 (36 years after the [[Model Parliament]]){{Cite web |title=Maldon {{!}} History of Parliament Online |url=http://www.histparl.ac.uk/volume/1386-1421/constituencies/maldon#constituency-main-article |access-date=2023-06-11 |website=www.histparl.ac.uk}} until 1707, then to the [[Parliament of Great Britain]] from 1707 to 1800 and to the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom]] from 1801. Under the [[Reform Act 1867|Reform Act of 1867]], its representation was reduced to one,{{Cite web |title=Representation of the People Act 1867 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1867/102/pdfs/ukpga_18670102_en.pdf |at=Schedule A}} and in 1885 the Parliamentary Borough was abolished and replaced with a Division of the County of Essex (later a County Constituency) under the [[Redistribution of Seats Act 1885]]. The constituency was abolished for the [[1983 United Kingdom general election|1983 general election]] following the [[Third Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies|Third Periodic Review of Westminster Constituencies]], but re-established for the [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010 general election]] by the [[Fifth Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies|Fifth Review]]. The current seat is primarily a successor to the [[Maldon and East Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|Maldon and East Chelmsford]] constituency which existed from 1997 to 2010. ==Boundaries and boundary changes== === 1885–1918 === * The Municipal Borough of Maldon; * The Sessional Divisions of Hinckford South (Braintree Bench) and Witham; and * Parts of the Sessional Divisions of Hinckford South (Halstead Bench), Lexden, and Winstree.{{Cite book|url=http://archive.org/details/publicgeneralac01walegoog|title=The public general acts|last=Great Britain|first=Incorporated Council of Law Reporting for England and Wales|publisher=Proprietors of the Law Journal Reports, 1884|others=unknown library|language=en}} ''Formally known as the Eastern or Maldon Division of Essex, incorporating the abolished Parliamentary Borough of [[Maldon, Essex|Maldon]] and extending northwards to include the towns of [[Witham]], [[Braintree, Essex|Braintree]] and [[Halstead]].'' === 1918–1950 === * The Municipal Borough of Maldon; * The Urban Districts of Braintree, Burnham-on-Crouch, and Witham; * The Rural District of Maldon; and * The Rural District of Braintree (including the detached part of the parish of Inworth which was wholly surrounded by the parishes of Great Braxted and Kelvedon).{{Cite book|url=http://archive.org/details/representationof00frasrich|title=The Representation of the people act, 1918 : with explanatory notes|last=Fraser|first=Hugh|date=1918|publisher=London : Sweet and Maxwell|others=University of California Libraries}} ''Area to the south between the rivers [[River Crouch|Crouch]] and [[River Blackwater, Essex|Blackwater]], including [[Burnham-on-Crouch]], transferred from the [[South East Essex (UK Parliament constituency)|South-Eastern Division of Essex]]. The northernmost area, including Halstead, and eastern fringes transferred to [[Saffron Walden (UK Parliament constituency)|Saffron Walden]] and [[Colchester (UK Parliament constituency)|Colchester]] respectively. Other minor changes.'' === 1950–1959 === * The Municipal Borough of Maldon; * The Urban Districts of Braintree and Bocking, Burnham-on-Crouch, and Witham; * The Rural District of Maldon; and * Part of the Rural District of Braintree.{{Cite book|title=Boundaries of parliamentary constituencies 1885-1972;|last=Craig, Fred W. S.|date=1972|publisher=Political Reference Publications|isbn=0900178094|location=Chichester|oclc=539011}} ''Marginal changes as a result of changes to local authority boundaries.'' === 1959–1974 === As above but the part of the Rural District of Braintree was altered by the County of Essex (Braintree and Lexden and Winstree Rural Districts) Confirmation Order 1955. ''Marginal changes as a result of changes to local authority boundaries.'' === 1974–1983 === * The Municipal Borough of Maldon; * The Urban District of Burnham-on-Crouch; and * The Rural Districts of Maldon and Rochford.{{Cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1970/1674/contents/made/data.htm|title=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 1970|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|access-date=2019-08-28}} ''Major reconfiguration, as Braintree and Bocking, and Witham, together with the parts of the Rural District of Braintree, formed the basis for the new constituency of [[Braintree (UK Parliament constituency)|Braintree]]. The Rural District of [[Rochford]] was transferred from [[South East Essex (UK Parliament constituency)|South East Essex]].'' Constituency abolished for the [[1983 United Kingdom general election|1983 general election]]. Southern area, comprising the former Rural District of Rochford, included in the new constituency of [[Rochford (UK Parliament constituency)|Rochford]].  Remainder formed the majority of the new constituency of [[South Colchester and Maldon (UK Parliament constituency)|South Colchester and Maldon.]]{{maplink|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Maldon (UK Parliament constituency) 2010}}|frame=yes|text=Map of boundaries 2010-2024}} === 2010–2024 === * The District of Maldon wards of Althorne, Burnham-on-Crouch North, Burnham-on-Crouch South, Heybridge East, Heybridge West, Maldon East, Maldon North, Maldon South, Maldon West, Mayland, Purleigh, Southminster, and Tillingham; and * The Borough of Chelmsford wards of Bicknacre and East and West Hanningfield, Little Baddow, Danbury and Sandon,Rettendon and Runwell, South Hanningfield, Stock and Margaretting, South Woodham Chetwood and Collingwood, and South Woodham Elmwood and Woodville.{{Cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2007/1681/made/data.htm|title=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 2007|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|access-date=2019-08-28}} ''Following the [[Boundary Commission for England|Boundary Commission]]'s [[Fifth Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], Parliament radically altered some constituencies and created new ones to allow for changes in population. The majority of the former [[Maldon and East Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|Maldon and East Chelmsford]] constituency formed the basis of this new seat for 2010. The constituency retained Maldon and Burnham-on-Crouch, but lost the Chelmsford parts to the re-established [[Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|Chelmsford]] seat and the new constituency of [[Witham (UK Parliament constituency)|Witham]]. To compensate, wards in and around [[South Woodham Ferrers]] were added from the former [[Rayleigh (UK Parliament constituency)|Rayleigh constituency]], and [[Margaretting]] was added from the former [[West Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|West Chelmsford constituency]].'' === Current === Further to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency was expanded northwards slightly with the transfer in from [[Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|Chelmsford]] of the City of Chelmsford ward of [[Galleywood]].{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule I Part 2 Eastern region}} ==The historic constituency (1332–1983)== {{Infobox UK constituency |name = Maldon |type = borough |parliament = uk |year = 1332 |abolished = 1885 |elects_howmany = two (1295–1868)
one (1868–1885) |previous = |next = |}} {{Infobox UK constituency |name = Essex, Maldon |type = county |parliament = uk |year = 1885 |abolished = 1983 |elects_howmany = one |previous = |next = |}} '''Maldon''' was originally a [[Parliamentary borough]] in [[Essex]], first represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] in 1332; it elected two MPs until 1868, and one from 1868 until 1885. In that year the borough was abolished but the name was transferred to a [[county division]] of Essex, which continued with some boundary changes until 1983. ===Maldon borough (1332–1885)=== ====Boundaries and franchise before the Reform Act==== Until the [[Great Reform Act]] of 1832, the borough consisted of the three parishes of the town of [[Maldon, Essex|Maldon]], a small market town and port on the coast of [[Essex]]. Maldon had been a municipal as well as a Parliamentary borough. Its first charter dated from the reign of [[Henry II of England|Henry II]], and at one time the corporation had the sole right to elect the town's MPs. From 1701 at the latest, however, the right to vote was exercised by the [[freedom of the city|freemen]] of the town, whether or not resident within the borough; and, unusually, honorary freemen and those acquiring the freedom by purchase were also entitled to vote in Maldon. This had several consequences. The electorate in Maldon was much bigger than was usual in a town of that size — in the first half of the 18th century, the number of qualified voters was generally about 800 (the majority of whom did not live in Maldon). It also meant that the town corporation, with the power to create freemen and therefore voters, was in a position to gerrymander elections if it so wished. This might, as was the case in some other boroughs, have ended in one interest gaining control of the corporation and turning Maldon into a [[pocket borough]]; in fact, however, Maldon instead stayed independent but venal, and gaining election there tended to be an expensive business. Sometimes it was not merely a case of bribing the voters: in 1690, it was recorded in the House of Commons journals that the wives and daughters of Maldon freemen were being bribed at election time as well. One interest that was firmly established by the middle of the 18th century, however, was that of the government, which ensured that lucrative posts in the customs house were reserved for loyally-voting freemen, and also attempted to have government supporters – often strangers to the town – elected to vacancies on the corporation. It was generally taken for granted that the government candidates would normally be elected. ====The Strutt ascendancy==== However, in the 1750s the government's control of Maldon weakened, and a prominent local [[British Tory Party|Tory]], [[John Strutt (1727–1816)|John Strutt]], found he had enough influence with the voters to sway elections. He secured the election of several of his friends over the years and eventually, in 1774, successfully stood for election himself. In the meanwhile, however, there was a dramatic change in the system. In 1763 one of the sitting MPs, Strutt's friend [[Bamber Gascoyne (the elder)|Bamber Gascoyne]], was appointed to the [[Board of Trade]] and therefore had to stand for re-election at Maldon. Gascoyne's opponent, [[John Huske]], accused him of threatening that any freemen working in the customs house who did not vote for him would be dismissed (which, by that time, would have been an illegal threat).Pages 109 to 113, [[Lewis Namier]], ''[[The Structure of Politics at the Accession of George III]]'' (2nd edition - London: St Martin's Press, 1957) Although the Prime Minister, [[George Grenville]], denied having authorised Gascoyne to make any such threat and Gascoyne denied having made it, it seems clear it was believed in Maldon and the corporation sided with Huske, creating enough new freemen to ensure Gascoyne was defeated. Both sides started actions for bribery, but Gascoyne had decided on more drastic action. He took out a writ against the corporation, and the Courts ordered the ousting of the majority of members; eventually, in 1768, the corporation was dissolved by judicial order. For half a century the duties of returning officer were transferred to the [[High Sheriff of Essex]]. However, the Sheriff could not assume the corporation's function of swearing in new freemen, and Strutt's influence was thus entirely secured against any possibility of new voters being created to outvote him. However, there was a problem: by the time of the [[1807 United Kingdom general election|general election of 1807]] the number of remaining qualified voters had dwindled to 58, and the constituency was in imminent danger of quite literally dying out. Yet there were more than 800 new freemen who were only barred from voting because there was nobody to swear them in. Finally a new charter was granted, in time to enfranchise them for the election of 1810. Matters then returned to normal in Maldon for the remaining 22 years before the [[Great Reform Act|Reform Act]]. Strutt's son, [[Joseph Holden Strutt]], retained much of the influence that his father had wielded, being generally considered to be able to nominate one of the two MPs or to choose to sit himself; as he exercised all government patronage in Maldon, he was well-placed to secure the other seat as well. But when the voters proved uncooperative, they could easily enough be overruled: at the [[1826 United Kingdom general election|1826 election]], the Corporation secured the result it wanted by admitting another thousand new freemen in time for them to vote: 3,113 freemen voted, of whom only 251 were Maldon residents. ====After the Reform Act==== In the initial drafts of the Reform Bill, Maldon was to lose one of its two seats. It was eventually spared this fate, but its population of 3,831 in 1831 left it very close to the borderline. The eventual Reform Act extended the borough by adding the neighbouring parish of [[Heybridge, Maldon|Heybridge]], increasing the population to 4,895; but with only 716 qualified voters under the new franchise its electorate was less than a quarter of what it had previously been. The constituency was a highly marginal one, victory rarely being secured by more than a handful of votes. In 1852, only 40 votes separated first place from fourth, and the second Tory's majority over his Whig opponent was only 6; after the losing candidates petitioned, alleging corruption, the election was declared void{{cite web|url=https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1853/mar/18/maldon-election|title=MALDON ELECTION|work=[[Hansard|Parliamentary Debates (Hansard)]]|date=1853-03-18|access-date=2009-05-04}} and Maldon's right to representation was suspended while a [[Royal Commission]] investigated. However, no major scandal was uncovered and (unlike some other boroughs similarly investigated at the same period) its right to vote was reinstated and a writ for a new by-election which took place in 1854 was issued.{{Cite web|url=https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1854/aug/11/new-writ-for-maldon|title=NEW WRIT FOR MALDON|work=[[Hansard|Parliamentary Debates (Hansard)]]|date=1854-08-11|access-date=2009-05-04}} ===Maldon county constituency (1885–1983)=== The [[Reform Act 1867|Second Reform Act]], implemented in 1868, took seats from most of the smallest boroughs, and Maldon's representation was halved; but it was still too small, and at the [[1885 United Kingdom general election|election of 1885]] the borough was abolished altogether. The [[county constituency|county division]] into which the town was placed, however, was named after the town. (Officially, until 1918, it was the '''Eastern (or Maldon) Division of Essex'''; after that, simply the '''Maldon''' division.) As well as Maldon itself this contained the towns of [[Braintree, Essex|Braintree]], [[Halstead]] and [[Witham]]. Once again this constituency was a marginal one — almost the only rural county seat in the South East at this period not to be safely [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]]. The strength of the Liberal vote seems to have been based partly on the strength of [[Nonconformist (Protestantism)|Nonconformism]] in the Halstead area, but also on trade unionism among the agricultural labourers (which elsewhere in Essex was offset by a strongly Tory maritime vote which Maldon lacked). [[Image:Maldon1918.png|right|thumb|260px|Maldon in Essex, 1918–1945]] After [[1918 United Kingdom general election|1918]], boundary changes added [[Burnham on Crouch]] and the surrounding district, but the constituency was still a rural one, with 35% of the occupied male population employed in the agricultural sector at the time of the 1921 census. The [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] Party rather than the Liberals were now the Conservatives' main opponents. When the Liberal Party split in 1922, Maldon's Liberals split as well, and the constituency was the first where the [[National Liberal Party (UK, 1922)|Lloyd George Liberals]] set up a constituency association, though this was apparently without the sanction of the national party headquarters and the association is not recorded as having organised any activities. In [[1923 United Kingdom general election|1923]] no Liberal candidate stood at all, and Labour captured the seat for the first time. The Conservatives retook the seat in [[1924 United Kingdom general election|1924]], holding it until the 1940s, but it was won by [[Tom Driberg]] in a wartime by-election; yet his hold on the seat was rarely secure and he eventually moved to sit for a safer seat. Thereafter Maldon remained Conservative until its abolition, though at first by the narrowest of margins. The Maldon constituency was abolished in the boundary changes which came into effect at the [[1983 United Kingdom general election|1983 election]], being divided between the new [[Colchester South and Maldon (UK Parliament constituency)|Colchester South and Maldon]] and [[Rochford (UK Parliament constituency)|Rochford]] constituencies. == Members of Parliament == ===MPs 1332–1640=== {{Expand [[Constituencies of the Parliament of the United Kingdom|constituency]] in [[Essex]]{{#tag:ref|A [[borough constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer).|group= n}} represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|UK Parliament]] since [[2017 United Kingdom general election|2017]] by [[Vicky Ford]] of the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]]. == History == Formally named as the Mid or '''Chelmsford''' Division of Essex, the seat was one of eight single-member divisions of Essex (later classified as county constituencies) created by the [[Redistribution of Seats Act 1885]], replacing the three two member divisions of East, South and West Essex. It continued in existence, gradually being reduced in geographic size as additional seats were created in Essex, until it was briefly abolished for the [[1997 United Kingdom general election|1997 general election]] following the [[Fourth Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies|Fourth Periodic Review of Westminster Constituencies]], when it was abolished and replaced by parts of two new constituencies: [[Maldon and East Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|Maldon and East Chelmsford]] and [[West Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|West Chelmsford]]. It was re-established for the [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010 general]] election as a Borough Constituency by the [[Fifth Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies|Fifth Periodic Review]]. During its latter years, the old seat was narrowly won by a [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] over strong [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrat]] performances, including their predecessor party the [[Liberal Party (UK)|Liberal Party]]. Historically, the constituency has on occasion been referred to as 'Mid Essex', especially in the early part of the 20th Century.{{cite web |url=http://venn.lib.cam.ac.uk/cgi-bin/search-2018.pl?sur=&suro=w&fir=&firo=c&cit=&cito=c&c=all&z=all&tex=RSC864FC&sye=&eye=&col=all&maxcount=50 |title=Frederick Carne Rasch Alumnus Record |website=University of Cambridge Alumni Print Records |publisher=[[University of Cambridge]] |access-date=June 22, 2020 |archive-date=24 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200624083618/http://venn.lib.cam.ac.uk/cgi-bin/search-2018.pl?sur=&suro=w&fir=&firo=c&cit=&cito=c&c=all&z=all&tex=RSC864FC&sye=&eye=&col=all&maxcount=50 |url-status=live }} At its first contest in 2010, the re-established seat was closely fought by the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats, who finished less than 10% apart, with Conservative candidate [[Simon Burns]] (the former MP for West Chelmsford) being elected. Labour polled 11%, despite having been only around 100 votes behind the Liberal Democrats in West Chelmsford in 2005, and even taking second place in 2001. Labour regained second place for the 2015 and 2017 elections but were overtaken again by the Liberal Democrats in 2019. == Boundaries and boundary changes == === 1885–1918 === * The Sessional Divisions of Brentwood (except the parishes of Rainham and Wennington) and Chelmsford.{{Cite book|url=http://archive.org/details/publicgeneralac01walegoog|title=The public general acts|last=Great Britain|first=Incorporated Council of Law Reporting for England and Wales|publisher=Proprietors of the Law Journal Reports, 1884|others=unknown library|language=en}} ''Formed from parts of the abolished [[West Essex (UK Parliament constituency)|West]] ([[Chelmsford]]), and [[South Essex (UK Parliament constituency)|South Divisions]], ([[Brentwood, Essex|Brentwood]] and [[Billericay (UK Parliament constituency)|Billericay]]).'' === 1918–1945 === * The Borough of Chelmsford; * The Urban District of Brentwood * The Rural Districts of Chelmsford and Ongar: and * The Rural District of Billericay parishes of Hutton, Ingrave, Mountnessing, Shenfield, and South Weald.{{Cite book|url=http://archive.org/details/representationof00frasrich|title=The Representation of the people act, 1918 : with explanatory notes|last=Fraser|first=Hugh|date=1918|publisher=London : Sweet and Maxwell|others=University of California Libraries}} ''Gained eastern part of the [[Epping (UK Parliament constituency)|Epping]] Division, including [[Chipping Ongar]]. The south-western corner, including [[Upminster]], was transferred to [[Romford (UK Parliament constituency)|Romford]] and southernmost parts, including the town of Billericay, to the [[South East Essex (UK Parliament constituency)|South-Eastern Division]].''[[File:Chelmsford1918.png|thumb|Chelmsford in Essex, showing boundaries used from 1918 to 1945]] === 1945–1950 === * The Borough of Chelmsford; * The Urban District of Brentwood; and * The Rural Districts of Chelmsford and Ongar.{{Cite book|title=Boundaries of parliamentary constituencies 1885-1972;|last=Craig, Fred W. S.|date=1972|publisher=Political Reference Publications|isbn=0900178094|location=Chichester|oclc=539011}} ''Minor changes following the reorganisation of local authorities, involving the abolition of the [[Billericay Rural District|Rural District of Billericay]] and the expansion of the [[Brentwood Urban District|Urban District of Brentwood]].'' [[File:Chelmsford1945.png|thumb|Chelmsford in Essex, showing boundaries used from 1945 to 1950]] === 1950–1955 === * The Borough of Chelmsford; and * The Rural Districts of Chelmsford and Ongar. ''Brentwood transferred to Romford.'' === 1955–1974 === * The Borough of Chelmsford; and * The Rural District of Chelmsford. ''The [[Ongar Rural District|Rural District of Ongar]] included in the new constituency of [[Chigwell (UK Parliament constituency)|Chigwell]].'' === 1974–1983 === * The Borough of Chelmsford; and * The Rural District of Chelmsford parishes of Danbury, East Hanningfield, Great Baddow, Highwood, Ingatestone and Fryerning, Little Baddow, Margaretting, Mountnessing, Rettendon, Runwell, Sandon, South Hanningfield, Stock, West Hanningfield, and Woodham Ferrers.{{cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1970/1674/contents/made/data.htm|title=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130162115/http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1970/1674/contents/made/data.htm|url-status=live}} ''Northern parts of the Rural District of Chelmsford transferred to the new constituency of [[Braintree (UK Parliament constituency)|Braintree]].'' === 1983–1997 === * The Borough of Chelmsford wards of All Saints, Baddow Road, Boreham and Springfield, Cathedral, Danbury and Sandon, East and West Hanningfield, Galleywood, Goat Hall, Great Baddow Village, Highwood and Margaretting, Little Baddow, Mildmays, Moulsham Lodge, Oaklands, Patching Hall, Rothmans, St Andrew's, Stock, The Lawns, and Waterhouse Farm.{{cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1983/417/contents/made/data.htm|title=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 1983|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|access-date=2019-08-30|archive-date=29 January 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190129122746/http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1983/417/contents/made/data.htm|url-status=live}} ''Gained the Boreham and Springfield ward from Braintree. Two parishes (Ingatestone and Fryerning, and Mountnessing), included in the District of Brentwood under the [[Local Government Act 1972]], were transferred to [[Brentwood and Ongar (UK Parliament constituency)|Brentwood and Ongar]]. South-eastern areas, including [[South Woodham Ferrers]], were included in the new constituency of [[Rochford (UK Parliament constituency)|Rochford]].'' For the 1997 general election the constituency was abolished. Northern and western areas forming the majority of the new constituency of [[West Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|West Chelmsford]]; eastern areas included in the new constituency of [[Maldon and East Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|Maldon and East Chelmsford]]; and a small area in the south included in the constituency of [[Rayleigh (UK Parliament constituency)|Rayleigh]]. {{maplink|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency) 2010}}|frame=yes|text=Map of boundaries 2010-2024}} === 2010–2024 === * The City of Chelmsford wards of Chelmer Village and Beaulieu Park, Galleywood, Goat Hall, Great Baddow East, Great Baddow West, Marconi, Moulsham and Central, Moulsham Lodge, Patching Hall, St Andrew's, Springfield North, The Lawns, Trinity, and Waterhouse Farm.{{cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2007/1681/made/data.htm|title=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 2007|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|access-date=2019-08-30|archive-date=20 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181120050742/http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2007/1681/made/data.htm|url-status=live}} Following the [[Boundary Commission for England|Boundary Commission's]] [[Fifth Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]] in 2007, Parliament re-established Chelmsford as a borough constituency for the [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010 general election]]. For the previous three elections the constituency had been split in two halves and included more surrounding rural settlements. A majority of the electorate for this new constituency came from the previous [[West Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|West Chelmsford constituency]]. A smaller element ([[Great Baddow]] and [[Galleywood]]) came from the [[Maldon and East Chelmsford (UK Parliament constituency)|Maldon & East Chelmsford constituency]]. The new constituency coincides with the built-up area which comprises the [[City of Chelmsford]]. === Current === Further to the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency was reduced to meet the electorate size requirements, with the transfer to [[Maldon (UK Parliament constituency)|Maldon]] of the [[Galleywood]] ward in the south of the city.{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 {{Short description|Parliamentary constituency in the United Kingdom, 2010 onwards}} {{Use dmy dates|date=June 2017}} {{EngvarB|date=June 2017}} {{Infobox UK constituency main |name = Clacton |parliament = uk |image = {{maplink|frame=yes|frame-align=center|plain=yes|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Clacton (UK Parliament constituency)}}|frame-height=200|frame-width=250}} |caption = Interactive map of boundaries from 2024 |image2 = [[File:East of England - Clacton constituency.svg|215px|alt=Map of constituency]] |caption2 = Boundary of Clacton in the East of England |year = 2010 |abolished = |type = County |previous = [[Harwich (UK Parliament constituency)|Harwich]] |next = |population = 85,359 (2011 census){{cite web |url=http://neighbourhood.statistics.gov.uk/dissemination/LeadTableView.do?a=7&b=6507826&c=&d=27&e=62&g=6430187&i=1001x1003x1032x1004&o=362&m=0&r=1&s=1422104706393&enc=1&dsFamilyId=2473|title=Clacton: Usual Resident Population, 2011 |website=Neighbourhood Statistics |publisher=Office for National Statistics |access-date=2 March 2015}} |electorate = 75,959 (2023){{cite web |url= https://boundarycommissionforengland.independent.gov.uk/2023-review/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition/the-2023-review-of-parliamentary-constituency-boundaries-in-england-volume-two-constituency-names-designations-and-composition-eastern/#lg_clacton-cc-75959 |title= The 2023 Review of Parliamentary Constituency Boundaries in England – Volume two: Constituency names, designations and composition – Eastern |publisher=Boundary Commission for England |access-date=26 June 2024 |df=dmy }} |mp = [[Nigel Farage]]
|party = Reform UK |region = England |county = [[Essex]] |european = East of England |towns = [[Clacton]], [[Frinton-on-Sea]] and [[Walton-on-the-Naze]] |elects_howmany = One }} '''Clacton''' is a [[Constituencies of the Parliament of the United Kingdom|constituency]]{{#tag:ref|A [[county constituency]] (for the purposes of election expenses and type of returning officer).|group= n}} in [[Essex]] represented in the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|UK Parliament]] since [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024]] by [[Nigel Farage]] of [[Reform UK]]. It is centred on the seaside town of [[Clacton]], hence its name. == Constituency profile == Clacton is almost completely coastal, comprising [[seaside resort]]s along the [[Tendring District|Tendring]] peninsula, including [[Clacton-on-Sea]], [[Frinton-on-Sea]] and [[Walton-on-the-Naze]]. It shares an inland boundary with just one constituency – [[Harwich and North Essex (UK Parliament constituency)|Harwich and North Essex]]. Similar to other coastal seats, such as [[Christchurch (UK Parliament constituency)|Christchurch]] in Dorset, Clacton's electorate comprises among the eldest in the country with a high proportion of [[Pensioner|retirees]] and not many non-white residents. The area has experienced a considerable influx of [[White British]] families from multicultural areas of [[East London]] such as [[Barking, London|Barking]] and [[Dagenham]], leading to the town of Clacton becoming known as "Little Dagenham".{{cite web |last=Easton |first=Mark |date=20 February 2013 |title=Why have the white British left London? |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-21511904 |publisher=BBC News}} The [[village]] of [[Jaywick]] was, in both the [[indices of deprivation 2010]] and 2015, identified as the single most deprived [[ONS coding system#Neighbourhood Statistics Geography|LSOA]] in England, out of around 32,000, with unemployment estimated at almost 50%. Many homes are essentially [[beach hut]]s and lack basic amenities. In 2018, Jaywick was visited by the [[United Nations special rapporteur]] for Poverty, [[Philip Alston|Professor Philip Alston]], as part of his examination into the causes of [[extreme poverty]].{{Cite news |date=2018-11-12 |title=Jaywick: UN poverty expert visits deprived village |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-essex-46178830 |access-date=2023-05-10}} Jaywick was named the most deprived place in the UK for the third consecutive year in 2019.{{Cite news |date=2019-09-26 |title=England's most deprived areas named as Jaywick and Blackpool |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-49812519 |access-date=2023-05-10}} [[Electoral Calculus]] categorises the seat as being part of the “Strong Right” demographic, those who have fiscally conservative views on the economy but are also fairly nationalist and socially conservative, alongside strong support for [[Brexit]]. Clacton is also, in general, highly [[multiple deprivation index|deprived]], in terms of employment, income and education, when measured comparatively with the rest of the UK, with 64% of the constituency being impoverished, according to the site.{{cite web |title=The Electoral Calculus’ profile of Clacton|url=https://www.electoralcalculus.co.uk/fcgi-bin/calcwork23.py?seat=Clacton |website=Electoral Calculus |access-date=12 June 2024}} In addition to this, the latest government labour data has also revealed that economic inactivity in Clacton is at 46.8% – more than twice the 21.7% UK average.{{cite web |title=Labour market data|url=https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/datasets/li02regionallabourmarketlocalindicatorsforparliamentaryconstituencies |website=Office for National Statistics |access-date=12 June 2024}} == History == Anciently under the jurisdiction of the [[Bishop of Rochester]] in [[Essex]] and part of the [[Baron Petre|Petre]] [[Estate (land)|estates]],[https://www.essexarchivesonline.co.uk/Result_Details.aspx?DocID=321518 www.essexarchivesonline.co.uk] the [[Legislature|seat]] of Clacton was established for the [[2010 United Kingdom general election|2010 general election]] following a [[Fifth Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies|review]] of parliamentary representation of [[Essex]] by the [[Boundary Commission for England]].{{Cite web |date=13 June 2007 |title=2007 No.1681 REPRESENTATION OF THE PEOPLE, ENGLAND REDISTRIBUTION OF SEATS The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 2007 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2007/1681/made |website=legislation.gov.uk }} It was formed out of the abolished [[Harwich (UK Parliament constituency)|Harwich constituency]], excluding the town of [[Harwich]] itself and surrounding areas. [[Douglas Carswell]], who was previously the [[List of Conservative Party MPs (UK)|Conservative MP]] for Harwich, won the seat at the 2010 general election. In August 2014, Carswell announced his defection to the [[UK Independence Party]] (UKIP) triggering [[2014 Clacton by-election|a by-election in the constituency]], winning with a large majority and thereby becoming [[UKIP]]'s first-elected MP. The then UKIP leader [[Nigel Farage]] declared that the result in Clacton had "shaken up British politics".{{Cite news |date=2014-10-09 |title=UKIP gains first elected MP with Clacton win |language=en-GB |publisher=[[BBC News]] |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-politics-29549414 |access-date=2023-05-10}} Carswell retained the seat at the [[2015 United Kingdom general election|2015 general election]]; this was the only constituency won by UKIP at the election. In March 2017, Carswell left UKIP to become an independent MP; he did not stand for re-election in the [[2017 United Kingdom general election|2017 general election]], when [[Giles Watling]] was victorious for the Conservatives. At the [[2019 United Kingdom general election|2019 general election]], Watling was re-elected with a majority of 24,702, increasing his vote share by 11.1% from 2017. Ahead of the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], it was announced that Nigel Farage, who had taken over as leader of [[Reform UK]] mid-campaign, would contest the Clacton constituency.{{cite news| url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3gg66pm8ylo |title=Farage enters election race as Reform UK candidate |publisher=[[BBC News]] |date=3 June 2024 |access-date=24 June 2024}} A [[YouGov]] poll published on 19 June 2024 (using the [[Multilevel regression with poststratification|MRP technique]]) predicted that Farage would defeat Watling.{{cite web |title=YouGov MRP projection|url=https://yougov.co.uk/politics/articles/49809-second-yougov-2024-election-mrp-shows-conservatives-on-lowest-seat-total-in-history |publisher=YouGov |date=19 June 2024 |access-date=24 June 2024}} Farage won the 2024 election with 46.2% of the vote.{{Cite web |date=2024-07-04 |title=Nigel Farage wins Clacton as Reform UK takes four seats |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c3gw83w8xg9o |access-date=2024-07-05 |website=BBC News |language=en-gb}} ==Boundaries== === 2010–2024 === {{maplink|raw={{Wikipedia:Map data/Clacton (UK Parliament constituency) 2010}}|frame=yes|text=Map of boundaries 2010–2024}} The [[Tendring District|District of Tendring]] [[Ward (electoral subdivision)|ward]]s of Alton Park, Beaumont and Thorpe, Bockings Elm, Burrsville, [[Frinton]], Golf Green, Hamford, Haven, Holland and Kirby, Homelands, [[Little Clacton]] and Weeley, Pier, Rush Green, St Bartholomews, St James, St Johns, St Marys, [[St Osyth]] and Point Clear, St Pauls and Walton.{{Cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2007/1681/made/data.htm|title=The Parliamentary Constituencies (England) Order 2007|website=www.legislation.gov.uk|access-date=2019-09-11}} The new seat consisted essentially of the former [[Harwich (UK Parliament constituency)|Harwich constituency]], minus the town of [[Harwich]] itself and a few nearby villages, plus [[St Osyth]] and [[Weeley]], transferred from the abolished [[North Essex (UK Parliament constituency)|North Essex constituency]]. === Current === Following the [[2023 Periodic Review of Westminster constituencies]], which came into effect for the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]], the composition of the constituency is as follows (as they existed on 1 December 2020): * The District of Tendring wards of: Bluehouse; Burrsville; Cann Hall; Coppins; Eastcliff; Frinton; Homelands; Kirby Cross; [[Kirby-le-Soken]] & Hamford; [[Little Clacton]]; Pier; St. Bartholomew’s; St. James; St. John’s; [[St Osyth]]; St. Paul’s; The Bentleys & Frating; The Oakleys & Wix; Thorpe, Beaumont & Great Holland; Walton; Weeley & Tendring; West Clacton & Jaywick Sands.{{Cite web |title=The Parliamentary Constituencies Order 2023 |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2023/1230/schedules/made |at=Schedule I Part 2 Eastern region}} ''The revised contents correspond to the existing constituency, expanded slightly by the addition of some inland rural areas and villages, transferred from [[Harwich and North Essex (UK Parliament constituency)|Harwich and North Essex]].'' ==Members of Parliament== ''[[Harwich (UK Parliament constituency)|Harwich]] prior to 2010'' {| class="wikitable" |- !colspan="2"|Election!!Member Farage]] | [[Reform UK|Reform UK]] |} The constituency's [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|Member of Parliament]] until 3 May 2017, was [[Douglas Carswell]], who had previously sat for the [[Harwich (UK Parliament constituency)|Harwich]] constituency since gaining that seat for the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservatives]] in [[2005 United Kingdom general election|2005]].{{cite web |url=https://members.parliament.uk/member/1527/career |title=Parliamentary Career for Mr Douglas Carswell |author= |date= |publisher=UK Parliament |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200422092149/https://members.parliament.uk/member/1527/career |url-status=live |archive-date=22 April 2020 |access-date=22 April 2020}}{{cite web |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/shared/vote2005/html/305.stm |title=Result: Harwich |author= |year=2005 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200422092347/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/shared/vote2005/html/305.stm |url-status=live |archive-date=22 April 2020 |access-date=22 April 2020}} On 28 August 2014, Carswell announced his defection to [[UK Independence Party|UKIP]].{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-28967904|title=Tory MP Douglas Carswell defects to UKIP and forces by-election|work=BBC News|date=28 August 2014 }} Although not required to seek re-election following a change of party allegiance, Carswell triggered a [[2014 Clacton by-election|by-election]], held on 9 October 2014, in which he was elected as the UKIP candidate.{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-29027997|title=Clacton by-election candidates|work=BBC News|date=2 September 2014 }} He became the first elected UKIP MP.{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-29549414 |title=UKIP gains first elected MP with Clacton win |author= |date=10 October 2014 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200422091814/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-29549414 |url-status=live |archive-date=22 April 2020 |access-date=22 April 2020}} Carswell retained the seat for UKIP at the [[2015 United Kingdom general election|2015 general election]], seeing his majority cut by roughly three-quarters, with an 11% swing to the Conservatives. Carswell then became UKIP's sole MP in the [[British House of Commons|House of Commons]], as [[Mark Reckless]], a fellow Conservative defector, lost [[Rochester and Strood (UK Parliament constituency)|his seat]].{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-32633719 |title=Nigel Farage resigns as UKIP leader as the party vote rises |author= |date=8 May 2015 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200422091501/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-32633719 |url-status=live |archive-date=22 April 2020 |access-date=22 April 2020}} On 25 March 2017, Carswell announced on his [[blog]] that he was quitting UKIP to sit as an independent MP,{{cite web |url=http://www.talkcarswell.com/home/job-done--thank-ukip/3237 |title=Job done – thank UKIP! |publisher=talkcarswell.com |date=25 March 2017 |access-date=25 March 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170325165657/http://talkcarswell.com/home/job-done--thank-ukip/3237 |archive-date=25 March 2017 |url-status=dead }} saying that "I switched to UKIP because I desperately wanted us to leave the EU. Now we can be certain that [[2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum|that is going to happen]], I have decided that I will be leaving UKIP".{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-39393213 |title=Douglas Carswell quitting UKIP to become independent MP for Clacton |author= |date=25 March 2017 |work=BBC News}} After [[Prime Minister of the United Kingdom|Prime Minister]] [[Theresa May]] called a [[2017 United Kingdom general election|snap election]] on 19 April 2017, Carswell announced that he would not stand for re-election and endorsed the Conservative Party candidate [[Giles Watling]].{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-politics-39655704|title=Douglas Carswell will not stand in general election|work=BBC News |date=20 April 2017|via=bbc.co.uk}} Watling was elected at the [[2017 United Kingdom general election|2017 general election]]; at that election, UKIP's share of the vote fell by 36.8%, one of its largest declines in the country, and the subsequent Conservative victory in Clacton marked the first time every constituency in [[Essex]] had returned a Conservative MP since [[1987 United Kingdom general election|1987]]. In [[2019 United Kingdom general election|2019]], Giles Watling, won re-election on the back of a majority of 24,702, increasing his vote share by 11.1% from 2017. ==Elections== === Elections in the 2020s === {{main|Clacton in the 2024 United Kingdom general election}}
